the marginal bid price is positively related to the genetic improvement in weaning weight of the offspring of the sire, the expected length of time the bull is used in the breeding herd, and the discount rate used to calculate the present value of future net revenues.
a beef herd owner should be willing to pay an additional $2.10 for each additional $1.00 increase in the average weaning weights (AWW) of his calves.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the economic analysis of genetic improvement programs in beef cattle production systems.
the economics of purchasing superior breeding stock.
determining the marginal bid price a producer is willing to pay for a genetically superior beef bull.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the case of a beef herd, the value of genetic improvements is not easily quantified.

the marginal bid price is a function of the after-tax net revenue of a beef herd, the cost of the current bull, the cost of purchasing the genetically superior bull, the genetic improvement expected from the genetically superior bull and the time period over which the expected genetic improvement would be realized.
the marginal bid price depends on the expected increase in weaning weights and the length of time the sire is used, the cost of the current herd sire and the interest rate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the marginal bid price is influenced by the magnitude of the expected genetic improvement in weaning weight, the expected rate of return on investment, and the number of offspring expected to be born from the bull.
a bull with an expected genetic merit for increased average weaning weight of $10.00 per calf is worth approximately $1,000 to the average cow-calf producer.
a producer should be willing to pay more for a superior breeding bull.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a producer can use the marginal bid price to determine the additional price they are willing to pay for a bull.
the marginal bid price increases as the expected improvement in weaning weight increases and the length of the breeding period increases.

producers should consider purchasing a genetically superior bull if their herd is currently producing below-average weaning weights and they have a reasonable expectation of being able to realize the expected genetic gain from superior bulls.
